title: Wrexham and Birmingham test star power in the Championship
excerpt: Hollywood-owned Wrexham broke records on the way up, while Tom Brady's Birmingham sit inside the Championship play-off places.
content_html:
Two of the most talked-about clubs in English football's second tier are chasing the Premier League with owners who made their names far from the pitch.

Wrexham are owned by Hollywood actors Ryan Reynolds and Rob McElhenney. Birmingham City count seven-time Super Bowl champion Tom Brady among their minority owners. Both clubs have drawn global attention, documentary crews and new fans. The question this season is whether that turns into promotion.

Wrexham's record climb

Since returning to the Football League in 2023, Wrexham became the first club in English football to win three promotions in a row, rising from the National League to the Championship. Manager Phil Parkinson was granted the Freedom of Wrexham County Borough for the run.

The fourth step proved harder. Wrexham finished seventh in their first Championship season on 71 points, one place outside what were then the play-off positions.

That finish would have been enough this season. EFL clubs voted to expand the Championship play-offs from four teams to six from 2026-27, so seventh place now earns a shot at promotion.

Birmingham in the mix

Birmingham have taken a quieter route. After 17 matches they are fourth on 32 points, which would put them straight into the play-off semi-finals under the new format. They are three points behind Middlesbrough and Stoke City, who hold the automatic promotion places.

The margins are tiny. Birmingham are level on points with fifth-placed West Bromwich Albion, and under the new format that one place matters: fourth goes straight to the semi-finals, while fifth has to win an extra knockout match.

Brady's involvement keeps the club in American headlines. Pundits have also urged Championship clubs to gamble on big-name free agents such as former England midfielder Dele Alli.

Does fame win matches?

Not on its own. Both ownership groups have invested in stadiums, training facilities and recruitment, and have backed their managers through difficult spells. Fame helps sell shirts and fill stadiums, but the investment behind it matters more on the pitch.

For Australian viewers who discovered English football through the series Welcome to Wrexham, the second half of the season offers two star-backed clubs chasing the same prize in the same league.
